To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the Internet mode does not systematically affect SP survey results, (ii) the Internet mode is not associated with lower response rates, and (iii) Internet surveys do not systematically suffer from higher measurement error.

(1) Internet surveys can provide reliable welfare estimates; (2) the quality of Internet responses is generally comparable to that of other modes; (3) Internet SP studies have been shown to produce welfare estimates that are equal to those obtained from other modes; and (4) there are some indications of lower welfare estimates in Internet surveys, but the evidence is not conclusive.

(1) Internet SP surveys are not different in quality from traditional SP modes; (2) Internet SP surveys may have lower response rates than other modes; (3) there is no clear relationship between response rate and quality of the responses, and therefore, (4) the choice of mode depends on the research objective.

the Internet mode should not be used in SP surveys without considering the implications for the validity and reliability of the results.
the choice between Internet and other survey modes should be based on practical and theoretical considerations, not on a priori beliefs about the quality of Internet SP surveys.
